title: ABIMELECH’S HOUSEHOLD WOMEN BECAME INFERTILE — And the Sarah Crisis Reveals What Happens When God Steps Into a Hidden Compromise
paragraphs: ABIMELECH’S HOUSEHOLD WOMEN BECAME INFERTILE — And the Sarah Crisis Reveals What Happens When God Steps Into a Hidden Compromise

Genesis 20:17–18 is more disturbing than it first appears. A frightened husband concealed the truth. A king unknowingly took another man’s wife. An entire household suddenly felt consequences it did not understand. Then one prayer changed everything. But beneath the scandal is something even greater: the relentless grace of a God who protects His promise when human beings make a complete mess of the story.
Imagine living inside Abimelech’s household.
Everything appears normal.
Then something begins happening among the women.
Pregnancies stop.
Wombs remain closed.
Something is wrong.
But nobody knows why.
No one can see the conversation that happened outside the palace. No one knows what Abraham said about Sarah. No one understands the danger hanging over the king’s house.
They only know something has changed.
And then Scripture gives us one of those sentences that can make you stop reading and stare at the page.
“For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham’s wife.”
Genesis 20:18.
The Hebrew is even more striking:
כִּי־עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה בְּעַד כָּל־רֶחֶם לְבֵית אֲבִימֶלֶךְ בְּעַד שָׂרָה אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָהָם
Ki-‘atzor ‘atzar YHWH be‘ad kol-rechem leveit Avimelekh, be‘ad Sarah eshet Avraham.

The construction עָצֹר עָצַר (‘atzor ‘atzar) intensifies the idea of restraining or closing. The text says that YHWH had closed “every womb”—כָּל־רֶחֶם (kol-rechem)—belonging to the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.
This was not merely an unfortunate fertility problem occurring in the background of the story.
Genesis explicitly connects what happened in Abimelech’s household to the Sarah crisis.
But before anyone turns this passage into a simplistic formula—“someone sins and therefore somebody becomes infertile”—we need to stay painfully close to the text.
Genesis 20 does not teach that infertility in general is evidence that someone has sinned.
It does not give Christians permission to look at a woman struggling to conceive and whisper, “What did she do?”
Please never weaponize this passage against someone carrying the private grief of infertility.
That would be cruel.
And it would be bad biblical interpretation.
Genesis is describing a specific divine intervention at a specific moment in redemptive history involving Abraham, Sarah, Abimelech, and the covenant promise of God.
And the circumstances that brought everyone there were messy.
Very messy.
Abraham had entered Gerar with Sarah.
And Abraham said something that should sound painfully familiar to anyone who has already read Genesis 12.
“She is my sister.”
Technically, there was truth buried inside the statement. Genesis 20:12 tells us Sarah was Abraham’s half-sister.
But Abraham was withholding the truth that mattered most.
She was also his wife.
That is what makes this story uncomfortable.
Abraham was not a cartoon villain.
He was the man God had called.
The man who believed God.
The man whose faith would become foundational to the biblical story.
And yet here he is...
afraid.
Again.
Abraham later explains his reasoning:
“Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife’s sake.”
Genesis 20:11.
Fear began writing the script.
And fear has written some terrible scripts in the lives of otherwise faithful people.
Fear says:
Tell enough truth to protect yourself.
Hide enough truth to control what happens next.
Make the compromise look reasonable.
Convince yourself you had no choice.
Have you ever done that?
Not necessarily with a king.
Not necessarily with a marriage.
But with your reputation?
Your browser history?
Your finances?
Your relationship?
Your addiction?
Your private conversations?
Your secret resentment?
Your spiritual life?
Have you ever constructed a version of the truth designed less to reveal reality and more to protect yourself from its consequences?
That is where this ancient scandal suddenly becomes uncomfortably modern.
Because some lies are spoken with completely false words.
Others are constructed from carefully selected truths.
Abraham’s fear placed Sarah in a devastating position.
Abimelech took Sarah into his household.
Then God intervened.
Before Abimelech slept with her, God came to him in a dream and gave him a terrifying warning:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man’s wife.”
Genesis 20:3.
Imagine hearing that from God.
Abimelech protested that he had acted without knowing the truth.
And remarkably, God acknowledged it.
God told him:
“Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.”
Genesis 20:6.
Do not miss that.
Abimelech did not know the entire situation.
God did.
Abraham had created confusion.
God entered the confusion.
Sarah was vulnerable.
God protected Sarah.
Abimelech was approaching an act whose full significance he did not understand.
God restrained him.
The covenant appeared endangered by human fear.
God did not lose control.
That is one of the great currents running beneath Genesis 20.
Human beings are making a mess.
God is preserving His purpose.
And perhaps that is where this story finds some of us.
You love Jesus...
but you have made a mess.
You knew better...
but fear won.
You believed God...
until the pressure became personal.
You trusted Him on Sunday...
then tried to manipulate the outcome on Tuesday.
You have a testimony, but there is a chapter you hope nobody reads.
Welcome to the uncomfortable honesty of Scripture.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes.
Abraham’s failures are left on the page.
Why?
Because ultimately the Bible is not a monument to the flawless performance of Abraham.
It is the revelation of the faithfulness of God.
And Genesis 20 refuses to let Abraham become the savior of his own story.
He needs grace too.
That matters enormously.
Because some people secretly believe Christianity is about good people proving they deserve God.
It is not.
The Gospel eventually brings us to exactly the opposite conclusion.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
Abraham needed grace.
Sarah needed God’s protection.
Abimelech needed warning.
His household needed healing.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And the ultimate answer is not Abraham.
It is Jesus Christ.
But watch what happens before we get there.
God tells Abimelech to return Sarah.
Then God says something surprising about the very man whose fear helped create the crisis:
“He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live.”
Genesis 20:7.
Read that again.
The compromised prophet is still called to pray.
That does not excuse Abraham.
Grace never means sin suddenly becomes righteous.
But God is already showing us something about restoration.
Failure does not have to be the final sentence.
Abimelech confronts Abraham.
Sarah is restored.
And then comes Genesis 20:17:
וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל אַבְרָהָם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּרְפָּא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וְאֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאַמְהֹתָיו וַיֵּלֵדוּ
Vayyitpallel Avraham el-ha’Elohim, vayirpa Elohim et-Avimelekh ve’et-ishto ve’amhotav, vayeledu.
“And Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.”
The verb וַיִּרְפָּא (vayirpa) comes from רפא (rapha’), “to heal.”
Abraham prayed.
God healed.
The closed wombs opened.
Life could continue.
The judgment was real.
So was the mercy.
That tension matters.
Modern Christianity can sometimes speak about grace as though grace means God simply shrugs at sin.
Genesis 20 will not allow that.
God takes wrongdoing seriously.
He identifies Sarah unmistakably as another man’s wife.
He warns Abimelech.
He restrains sin.
He requires Sarah’s restoration.
There are consequences inside the household.
And yet judgment is not where the story ends.
Healing comes.
Restoration comes.
Mercy comes.
That is why the Gospel is so much greater than pretending our scandals never happened.
Jesus does not save us by rewriting history so that we were secretly innocent all along.
He saves sinners.
At the cross, sin is not called harmless.
It is exposed as so serious that redemption costs the blood of Christ.
And grace is revealed as so astonishing that the Son of God willingly gives Himself for sinners.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
The scandal of Genesis 20 therefore whispers toward the greater story Scripture will eventually unveil.
Human failure.
Divine intervention.
Judgment.
Mercy.
Restoration.
And ultimately...
Christ.
There is another detail we cannot ignore.
Sarah is not merely Abraham’s wife.
She stands inside the unfolding covenant promise.
God had already declared that Sarah would bear Isaac.
Genesis 17:19 says:
“Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed; and thou shalt call his name Isaac: and I will establish my covenant with him.”
Then in Genesis 18, God again promises that Sarah will have a son.
And suddenly, in Genesis 20, Sarah is inside another king’s household.
Do you see the narrative tension?
God has promised a son through Abraham and Sarah.
Yet Abraham’s fear creates circumstances that could throw the identity and integrity of the promised line into confusion.
But God intervenes before Abimelech touches her.
The promise will not be hijacked by Abraham’s fear.
The covenant will not collapse because the covenant bearer panicked.
God remains faithful even when human faithfulness trembles.
Then Genesis 21 begins.
“And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.”
As He had said.
As He had spoken.
That is the heartbeat.
God keeps His word.
Not because Abraham performed perfectly.
Not because Sarah never struggled.
Not because every human decision was wise.
God keeps His word because God is faithful.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction.
God’s faithfulness is not permission to continue living in compromise.
It is the reason you can repent without believing your story is over.
Repentance is not running away from grace.
Repentance is turning toward the God of grace.
Maybe you have been carrying something.
Something you have learned to hide so well that people compliment the version of you they see while you quietly grieve the person you know exists underneath.
Maybe there is an Abraham-sized compromise hiding inside a respectable Christian life.
Maybe fear made you dishonest.
Maybe loneliness made you vulnerable.
Maybe lust became a secret room.
Maybe bitterness became your companion.
Maybe pride made repentance feel humiliating.
Maybe you keep saying, “It’s complicated,” because calling it sin would mean admitting something needs to change.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to hide better.
The answer is Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
There is no freedom in endlessly protecting the version of yourself that is killing your fellowship with God.
Bring it into His light.
Name the sin.
Stop negotiating with it.
Stop dressing bondage in respectable language.
Repent.
Not because Christ is waiting for an excuse to destroy you.
Because Christ died and rose again to save sinners.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is reconciliation with God through Christ.
There is a new life that does not require you to pretend the old wounds never existed.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful things about Genesis 20 is that the chapter does not end with closed wombs.
It ends with healing.
Think about that.
The scandal was real.
But so was the restoration.
Abraham’s fear was real.
But it did not become sovereign.
The crisis was real.
But the crisis did not get the last word.
God did.

That is the message Gospel Warrior exists to keep declaring in a world full of hidden wounds, exhausted believers, skeptical seekers, prodigals, struggling Christians, and people who think their worst chapter has permanently disqualified them:
Jesus Christ still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus still restores broken people.
Jesus still turns shame into testimony.
Jesus still takes stories that look ruined and writes redemption across pages we thought were finished.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest before God.
And if you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you are exhausted but you have not abandoned Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your spirit has been worn thin and you desperately need prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody reading underneath this article may need evidence that Christians are not people without scars—we are people whose scars no longer have to tell the story without the cross.
Do not make the comments a performance.
Make them a place of honesty.
There is still grace.
Save it too.
There are truths you do not save because you have forgotten them.
You save them because there will be days when pain tries to make you forget.
Scripture deserves greater care than that.
The New Testament principle for Christian giving is beautifully free of manipulation:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
2 Corinthians 9:7.
God’s grace is not for sale.
If Gospel Warrior has strengthened you, your monthly support helps us keep building and expanding the work so more people can encounter biblical truth and be pointed toward Christ.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel ministry is not merchandise.
It is mission.
It is another article reaching a broken person.
Another devotional reaching someone fighting temptation.
Another Christian resource strengthening a believer.
Another seeker hearing that Christianity is not fundamentally the story of human beings becoming impressive enough for God.
It is the story of the holy God coming to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
And whether you are able to support financially or not, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Because ministry is not ultimately measured by how impressive a page looks.
It is measured by faithfulness to Christ and by whether people are being pointed toward Him.
Genesis 20 began with fear.
It moved through deception.
A woman was placed in danger.
A king received a terrifying warning.
A household experienced closed wombs.
A prophet who had failed was confronted.
Then Abraham prayed.
God healed.
Sarah was restored.
And the promise continued.
Then the next chapter opened with words every wounded believer should remember:
“The LORD visited Sarah as he had said.”
As He had said.
Maybe that is the sentence you need tonight.
Your failure is not more powerful than God.
Your secret is not too dark for the light of Christ.
Your shame does not possess greater authority than the blood shed at Calvary.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance makes yesterday nonexistent.
It means that when a sinner turns to Jesus Christ, yesterday no longer has the authority to determine eternity.
So come out of hiding.
Bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear from the book.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the thing you cannot repair yourself.
And trust the Savior who was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
Because the most unforgettable truth in Abraham’s scandal is not that Abraham nearly ruined everything.
It is that God remained faithful.
And the most unforgettable truth about your story may not be what you did in the chapter you are ashamed of.
It may be what Jesus did after you finally surrendered the pen.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the risen Christ is still writing redemption.
